newsitem.title: USA: USDA hosts conference on world food security.
newsitem.headline: USDA hosts conference on world food security.

text.p: Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman and other U.S. policy, academic and industry leaders met Wednesday to discuss world food security and begin developing a U.S. action plan to alleviate the problem of hunger globally and inside the United States.

As a follow-up to the World Food Summit held last year in Rome, discussions were held simultaneously Wednesday at 15 sites around the country to focus on ways to address hunger and malnutrition at home and abroad. On June 5, the results of the consultations will be discussed in Washington to develop a draft outline for the U.S. plan.

Glickman and other officials said that it is not enough to merely throw food aid at problem areas, but that nations must develop domestic economies, improve infrastructure and enact free-market reforms to alleviate food shortage problems.
"It is readily apparent today that we can no longer afford to simply throw food at the problem -- nor is that any kind of long-term solution," said Glickman.
Glickman said that if foreign leaders enact free-market reforms and make other improvements, "they can expect assistance from the world in building up their agricultural base."

Glickman also noted that hunger is a problem in the United States and that domestic feeding program should be fully funded. He also said that quality education needs to be provided to people to break the cycle of poverty and hunger and create more opportunities for lower-income individuals.

U.S. Agency for International Development administrator Brian Atwood said that governments that have been the most successful in establishing food security have pursued sound economic policies and invested in health, education and agricultural research.

Atwood pointed out that despite misconceptions that the U.S. government spends 20 percent of its budget on foreign aid, less than half of one percent of the national budget goes to foreign assistance -- putting the United States at the bottom of the industrialized countries on what it contributes -- on a per capita basis -- to foreign economic assistance.

Atwood said AID pursues food security through an integrated approach, using agricultural programs, development assistance and food aide, with a strong emphasis on those countries that "show a good-faith willingness to adopt necessary policy reforms."
